title: Playing silent-film scores for Erskine Tate at the Vendome
summary: Describes the theater pit, picture scores, hand-signal themes and fast cuts between numbers.

story.theme_name: Medicine shows, minstrels, circuses and the black theater circuit
story.community_name: On the road with minstrel, carnival and tent shows

blocks.x: What sort of music did you play with Tate?
Like I say, we played for silent

pictures. Played all kinds, played jazz, classical, overtures, and quite naturally, we had to play for the pictures, so we had to play -- they sent out a release -- when they sent a picture out during the week, they'd send a score with it. And you had to have all these different numbers in the score in order to play for the picture. Because the librarian, he'd see-me to work early and watch the picture and watch the score and set up the numbers. And then when we'd come to work, we had to set up the numbers according to the picture.
You mean the arrangements?
The arrangements, yeah.
And you'd have to go from one to the other?
One to the other, and you didn't get a chance to play a full one. Sometimes you didn't get a chance to play but two or three bars.
That was pretty hard work.
Oh, yes it was. But it's real fascinating for a young fellow.
(Laughter.)
(Inaudible).

Yeah, had to watch the conductor, see, because you had -- like you'd have a five finger theme, four finger theme, two finger theme. And he watched the picture, and the minute the scene changes, he'd cut the band off. You'd be right in the middle. Then he'd hold up five fingers, and

then you'd go to your five finger theme. Thumb theme, he'd hold up a thumb. You go to the thumb theme. You had music all over your rack. So you could grab it at a moment's notice, see. Then he'd take the stick and cut the band off. You had to cut. Then he'd hold up his five fingers, and you'd go pick that up, put it in, and he'd start off and you'd start playing that for a little while. Then maybe there's a big fight coming, or something. Cut. Then you go into your hurry, what you call hurry, hurry number one, two, number three, number four, number five.
Like a gallop.
The gallop, yeah. Oh, it was real fascinating.
And these were hand signals?
Yeah, the conductor, you know.
Or numbers of the parts.
Uh-huh.
Well, did you play in the pit? Well, sure, you would play in the pit for the movies. Did you also play on the stage?
Well, that was when I went to the Regal. That was later.
Uh-huh. But Tate's band --
Tate's band, we only had -- we didn't have a stage.
I see. Because he's fairly well-known, you know, as a theater band.
Yeah. Well, we had to do our O's and everything from the pit.
You had to do what?
We had to do the overture, and everything, from the pit.
I see. Do you recall who was in Tate's band at this time?
Oh --
And when was this, about 19 --
This was in 1928.
1928 when I started with Tate.
